title: IRB Decision 2000canlii21315

LA COMMISSION DE L’IMMIGRATION ET DU STATUT DE RÉFUGIÉ (SECTION DU STATUT DE RÉFUGIÉ) IMMIGRATION AND REFUGEE BOARD (REFUGEE DIVISION) File/Dossier: A98-01069 HUIS CLOS IN CAMERA DEMANDEUR CLAIMANT XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX DATE DE L'AUDIENCE DATE OF HEARING November 8, 2000 April 3, 2000 February 4, 2000 June 22, 1999 LIEU DE L'AUDIENCE PLACE OF HEARING Ottawa, Ontario DATE DE LA DÉCISION DATE OF DECISION November 8, 2000 November 16, 2000 (Reasons signed) CORAM CORAM XXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX POUR LE DEMANDEUR FOR THE CLAIMANT XXXXXXXXXXXXX Barrister and Solicitor AGENT CHAXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX ION REFUGEE CLAIMS OFFICER

2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
1 A98-01069 
 The following is our decision and reasons for deci sion rendered from the bench in the claim of XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, whom we found not to be a Convention Refugee. This text has been edited for clarity in written form. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, Presiding Member XXXXXXXXXXXXX, the Panel is in a position to render a decision in your claim. We arrive at our decision after having given careful consideration to all the written evidence before us as well as your testimony over a number of sittings. We first met on the 22nd of June 1999. You testified for over three hours that day. We next met on the 4th of February 2000 with your counsel and provided for the disclosure of some information. And then we met with you again for about an hour on the 3rd of April 2000. Your evidence is that you are a citizen of Djibouti, where you were born in 1949. In the Port of Entry Notes, of which we have a record at Exhibit M1, the information provided is as follows: that you have four children, who were all at the tim e in Ethiopia; that you had a sister in Ottawa, residing at XXXXXXX with a telephone number of XXXXXX; that you travelled to Ottawa via the United States; that you fear persecution in Djibouti as a member of a political organization, that is to say, on the grounds of political opinion; and that you were a member of the PND. You were questioned about this, and you said th at you had not known your sister's address in Canada until strangers you met disembarking a plane in Washington provided you with this information. You also said that you are illiterate, that you had no knowledge of the contents of the Port of Entry form, nor any knowledge of why there would be any reference to any political affiliation. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
2 A98-01069 
 In your Personal Information Form, which we have before us at Exhibit C1, these are the essential assertions you make: You say that you are a member of the Midgan clan. You say that you had worked as a house cleaner and vegetable seller. You say that you were raped at age 15 by a man who was a cousin to the family for which you cleaned house. You say that in 1978 you opened a vegetable counter in the market. You say that in 1979, you married a Midgan man whose work was to repair car bodies, in an auto body shop. You say that your husband was harassed by police who demanded that he repair their cars for free. You say that your children endured insults and beatings as Midgans. You add that your son was injured in the course of an argument with authorities over the auto body business. You say that your husband died as a result of a savage beating by police who took over his car business. You say that in January 1998, you lost your vegetable business, and in March of 1998, you went with your four children to Ethiopia. They stayed there, but you were there only between April and August 1998. Finally, you say that your husband's friend assist ed you in getting you to Canada, obtaining the U.S. visa and arriving here to make a claim. In the course of our hearings, you were que stioned by your counsel, by the Refugee Claim Officer, as well as by the Panel members. There was conflict in your evidence regarding contact with your sister. You said that she lived in Djibouti and that you last saw her two months before you left the country. She left before you. You said that the people who brought you to Canada were involved in providing you with information with regard to her location. There was conflicting testimony as to whether it was two or three people with whom you arrived to Canada, and exactly whether you knew that your sister was here prior to arrival or not. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
3 A98-01069 
 In connection with the Midgan aspect of the claim that you had originally put forward, you recounted how you were raped at age 15. You said how you had a hard life cleaning house, how you were abused because you were a Midgan. You weren't compensated and whatnot. You married, you said, in 1979. At first you said 1997, but then you corrected that to 1979, and you said, in fact, your husband was killed in 1979. This is what you were saying up until we met today. In your Personal Information Form, you actually gave the date of your husband's death as 1997, rather than 1979. As I was saying, in your Personal Information Form at question 15, with regard to your husband, XXXXXXXXXXXXX, you say he was killed in 1997. You explained that while he had been in business for about 20 years, he took whatever abuse was handed his way by police. He was a Midgan, after all, and he couldn't really complain when they demanded free work. It was on an occasion in 1997 when he finally stood up to the police, and demanded to be paid. The policemen refused and that resulted in your husband being beaten, and, ultimately, his death two days later and problems for your son as well. You described in detail your experiences as a Midgan, the problems that you had. You also provided in support of that assertion an identity card issued by the French, that is to say, prior to Djibouti's independence, in which your husband's name appears and shows that he is an "autochtone", which is the French word for "native". And you said, "Well, that means he is a Midgan." You described typical Midgan occupa tions to support your assertion that you are Midgan too. It is also well known to us, and I believe you said it too, that non-Midgans never marry Midgans, so the fact that he was your husband would itsel f indicate since he was a Midgan that you were a Midgan. That is what you were saying up until today. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
4 A98-01069 
 You told us that you had reported your husband's death to the authorities, but they were unresponsive. You say that authorities came demanding money from you. You had no money. You depended on others as a Midgan, and that's why you left Djibouti. You said that a man came and threatened you, "If you don't leave us alone, you will face difficulties." That is in relation to your complaint against the police who had allegedly killed your husband. Regarding your Personal Information Form, you testified that an interpreter, XXXXXXXXX or XXXXXXXXXX, was the person who assisted you with it. You also told us that a woman named XXXXXXXX had referred you to Mr. XXXXXX. As to how you could afford the cost of travel to the United States and Canada, you said that a former employer of yours, someone who you had worked for 20 years before, had loaned you these funds. As far as your passport is concerned, which was issued in XXXXXX 1997, you said that you got it after your husband was beaten. You also indicated that police harassed you in the marketplace. They wanted money for khat. You were questioned with regard to your own visa application, but also your sister's U.S. visa application as well as that of her husband. You said a Somali man helped you fill out your application. As far as your sister was XXXXXXXXXX, you said your sister's husband was the owner of a small store and soldiers destroyed it. That's what you said, and that came up in today's hearing where you said that, in fact, you were simply responding to a question. You hadn't actually asserted that. You also told us that with regard to your own visa application, which appears as 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
5 A98-01069 
 Exhibit R2, the information contained in it is false. That's what the story was up until about 9:30 this morning. At today's resumption, today being November 8th, 2000, you, being aware of admissions of misrepresentation made by your sister in her own claim, admitted that you had provided the Panel with substantial false information. Together with counsel, we went through your Personal Information Form narrative paragraph by paragraph, having in mind the testimony that you had given in support of that story over four or five hours of viva voce evidence, and this is what we have found and what you acknowledged: The first paragraph of your narrative says your name, says that you are a citizen of Djibouti and born in 1949. All that is fine, but you say that you belong to the Midgan tribe, and you provide your subclan within the Midgans, how the Midgan tribe "are the least minority in the country" and how all the troubles you have arise from being a Midgan. "Somali people make it a normal practise to outcast Midgans, and my people are mistreated by the Somalis." That is what you say, and by your admission today, obviously you say that you are not a Midgan. In fact, you are an Issa-Fourlaba. We have other evidence that I will talk about that shows that your late husband was an Issa-Mamassan. That evidence that you provide today with regard to the truth of your own clan, the truthful identity of your own clan, eliminates the information in paragraph 1, other than that of your name, that you are a citizen of Djibouti and when you were born. We come to paragraph 2. I won't quote it, but in paragraph 2 you say, "I have lived a slavery childhood." Those are the words in the PIF. You talk about how tough your life was. You talk about how you were mistreated, and you make it a point to emphasize that Midgans have no rights of any kind in the country, and that's in your testimony, not only in your PIF. You attributed your problems as a house cleaner and the abuse that you suffered to being a Midgan. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
6 A98-01069 
 Well, of course, since you are not a Midgan, none of that makes any sense. In fact, you told us today that you did work as a house cleaner, but you were paid regularly and that you had no particular problems other than being shouted at occasionally by your employers. You took care of their children. You cleaned house. With regard to paragraph 3 of your Personal Information Form, you told us today that you were not raped when you were 15. In fact, nothing of that sort happened to you all the while that you were keeping house. So your testimony today in connection with those two paragraphs and the earlier testimony that you gave orally is also set aside because it's untruthful. We come to the next paragraph. You say in 1978 you opened a vegetable counter in the central market and you suffered aggression of the police who knew that you were a Midgan. Well, again, if you weren't a Midgan, then you couldn't have suffered aggression on that account. You did tell us, however, that you did have problems with the police. Why? Because you operated a vegetable stand without a permit. The police would harass you and chase you and other non-permit holders out of the market or demand money, bribe money, to let you stay. So again, while you may have had problems with the police, it was for lack of a permit. They were doing their job chasing non-permit holders out, and if you weren't inclined to pay the bribe to let them overlook your lack of a permit, well then you would get chased like the others. But it had nothing to do with being a Midgan or a woman or anything else. It had to do with working without a permit. With regard to paragraph 5, you say you got married in 1979. Your husband had an auto-body shop, and that theme goes on through paragraphs 5 through 11 inclusive, plus paragraph 15. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
7 A98-01069 
 You acknowledged that in their entirety, those paragraphs are false. You aren't a Midgan. Your husband was not a Midgan. He did not have an auto-body shop. And since everything in these paragraphs 5 through 11, and then 15 depend on him having had an auto-body shop, none of that evidence can stand as true. That essentially eliminates your claim. But you told us today that that in your situation, while you had indeed made this misrepresentation, in fact you still had a fear of returning to Djibouti. You told us that your eldest son was hurt in a car accident, which you feel was not such an accident, but was intentional, and as a result, he was disabled. We have a medical report, which was filed for the courts in Djibouti in XXXXXX 1993, at Exhibit C6, in connection with your son's injuries. I will note for the record that Exhibit C6 was only presented to us at the end of your testimony today, even though this document was obviously in your possession for a very long time, since XXXXXX 1993, in fact, long before you even came to Canada. With regard to this document and other documents filed today, your evidence is that the interpreter, XXXXXXXXX, had told you not to bother with these, and as a result, you didn't bother with them. You told us that you did seek compensation, or your son sought compensation for his injuries through the courts, and that was in 1993, but the courts did not serve him well. In fact, you said that the respondent in the case was a son of a cabinet minister and that the government interfered on his behalf in the court case, so your son could not get the compensation he wanted. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
8 A98-01069 
 You also told us today that between 1980 and 1983 you were employed with the airline and that your boss sexually harassed you. He wanted to have sex with you, and you would refuse, and as a result, in 1983 you were fired. I will note for the record that there is no reference in your Personal Information Form to your having worked for the airline in 1980 to 1983. You told us as well that you were a member of the PND, a Djiboutian opposition political party, and you presented us with a membership card, which we have at Exhibit C8. You also told us that the PND was not active now, that the leader works in his home. You also told us that the last PND event of any significance that you attende d was five or six years ago. You said it was before the last election, and you in fact specifie d, the election in which XXXXX was involved. In our documentary evidence at Exhibit R1, Tab 3, page 1, we see that that election in fact took place on the 7th of May 1993. That means that the last significant PND event you took place in was in 1993. You did say that you continued to e involved. You said that you got your current membership card, which we have at Exhibit C8, in 1998. Alas, I will point out that the card says that it was issued in 1997. As to what you fear if you were to return, you said what you fear is having more of the hard life that you had when you left, and you specifically talked about your life of hardship, your husband's death, your son's disability. Your husband had been dead for a long time. I think you said 23 years. Your youngest son was just six m onths old when his father died. So you have been a widow for a long time and life has been hard. I have already engaged in some degree of analysis of your evidence, certainly going to credibility, in the course of my recounting your evidence, but I would like to now more properly deal with the evidence by way of a more formal analysis. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
9 A98-01069 
 Your credibility overall is called into question by your admission of having presented a false claim. You testified today that the reason you presented a false claim is because this was the story which XXXXXXXXX, the interpreter, had provided for you and told you to tell. You also said he told you to forget about your documents, including the PND card. While you apologized for lying and said that you regret that you lied, in our view, that regret is at best quite limited. The reason I say that is that you have had representation through a capable counsel for many months. You were not truthful to him nor to us. Y ou have had lots of opportunity to reflect on the falsehoods that you have been presenting. Beyond that, you told us you know what happened in your sister's claim. You know that your sister had admitted to not being a Midgan, but rather, being an Issa-Fourlaba. You know that her cl aim failed, and I know that her claim failed two months ago or more because I was the member who heard that claim. You would have known that too because you are in touch with your sister . You knew what happened in her claim, so I imagine you would have heard of it, but it's not like we were advised any time before this morning that there was any acknowledgement on your part of any misrepresentation. All of that suggests to us that, again, you might regret some aspects of what you have done, but that there is no principled and deep-felt regret over the misrepresentation because otherwise it would have been corrected long ago. That being aside, in addition to your own false information provided in your PIF and as well over a number of prior sittings, you also provided us during those same sittings with false information about your sister and about your sister 's husband. You said that he was the owner of a small store destroyed by the military. Counsel even talks about that in submissions that he made once before, before new evidence came to light. In fact, today you acknowledge that he 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
10 A98-01069 
 was an official at the Hôpital XXXXX, the c ountry's XXXXX hospital. In fact, we have evidence before us at Exhibit R5, I believe, that tells us that he was the XXXXX since 1995-96 and continued to be to date", which is April 2000. That is, you had an influential relative who is still in the country, at least until April 2000. You also admitted today that you had provided false information with regard to your children's birth dates. The dates that we have in your Personal Information Form at question 15 are not true. Your oldest son was born, I think you sa id, in 1970, not 1980, and it flows from there, so even in information that one might say is certainly not central to your claim, you are prepared to misrepresent. For that matter, you had even testified on earlier occasions that you didn't know that your sister was in Canada, or you knew she wa s here, but not where she lived. By virtue of today's testimony, you have acknowledged that in fact you did know that she was here. In fact, you told us with regard to the Port of Entry Notes, contrary to what you had asserted before, you provided all the information that was in those fo rms, which means that you provided your sister's address. With regard to the PND, you did not testify to having had any problems on account of being involved in the PND except for being chased by police, together with a lot of other people, when they sought to disperse a PND meeting prior to the 1993 elections. Fundamentally, you could not clearly identify any agents of persecution. What you say, effectively, is that you fear a hard life on account of having no husband and a disabled eldest son who now lives in Ethiopia. You said your situation is different from that of your sister who has a husband. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
11 A98-01069 
 I must say, and I am speaking on behalf of the Panel, of course, that the extent of the misrepresentation in your claim taints the entire body of your evidence. We are prepared to accept that you had a hard life that resulted from difficult circumstances. Just being a widow would be hard enough. But you were able to raise four children. You were able to go to court. You weren't satisfied with the outcome. I can understand that. But that is really your son's problem. He is the one who sought the compensation and the one who needed it. It is a mother's pain to see her son in a difficult situation. As far as the PND is concerned, you say that you were involved, but we have that problem with the date of the issue of the membership card. We doubt that you are a PND member. Even if you are, and it is within our specialized knowledge that party membership cards from opposition parties are quite easy to come by, because opposition parties are all desperate for members, one can become a nominal member quite easily. Even if you are a PND member, you reported no problems arising therefrom. Even accepting that your son was involved in an accident -- you say it was a cabinet minister's son -- we don't have any evidence of that before us other than your assertion. You say he didn't get what he wanted from the courts, but we don't have the outcome of the court decision. We just have a medical report filed with the court. Even if we were to believe what you say about the outcome of the court process and even if we were to believe what you say about who was behind the accident, again, those are your son's problems fundamentally. It may cause you distress. Even if we were to believe that you were a member of the PND, you didn't report any ill effects. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
12 A98-01069 
 All of this leads us to find that you have not experienced persecution in the past, as that term is understood in the Convention and in Canadian jurisprudence. You have not experienced persecution as a woman in the past, nor as a PND member in the past, as that term persecution is understood in the Convention and Canadian law. Again, I will note that what you say you fear is effectively a hard life. But fundamentally, you ar e a member of a large and prominent tribe. Your late husband was a member of the most prominent subclan of the most prominent tribe, and implicit in your testimony today is that you did not suffer any persecution on account of being Issa-Fourlaba or on account of your husband be ing a Mamassan even though, as you put it, not all Mamassan are equal. We do know from our documentary evidence, however, that the Fourlaba are in a favourable position in Djibouti and that Mamassan, even the lesser of those, are in quite a favourable position in Djibouti, although as individuals, individuals may find themselves in trouble like anywhere else. Now, to be thorough the Panel did contemplate the possibility of a claim being made out on the basis of your gender. You are a woman. However, your own evidence of your past experiences do not suggest that you faced persecution in a Convention sense on that ground, and the documentary evidence at page 9 of Tab 1 of Exhibit R1, likewise, does not support a finding that there would be a reasonable chance that you would face persecution on that ground either. There is discrimination against women in areas such as inheritance, divorce and travel. You haven't provided any indication of problems. You did travel. You came here. Your husband wasn't available to give you permission, but you were able to do it nonetheless. There is no issue for divorce for you. So while as a woman returning to Djibouti you may or may not face some 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
13 A98-01069 
 forms of discrimination, or in fact you may face some forms of discrimination, it is not such as would amount to persecution in a Convention sense. You haven't argued that you face a denial of employment. As I said, you have told us that you would return to a life of hardship, the likes of which you have experienced for some time. We are sympathetic to the problems faced by widows. We are sympathetic to a mother's pain over the injury and disability experienced by an eldest son, but the Convention is forward looking. We have already found that the evid ence that you provided does not suggest past persecution on any Convention ground, and in looking forward, the evidence that you have provided to us, the fears that you have stated, do not suggest that you face more than a mere possibility of persecution in Djibouti on any Convention ground should you return there. Those being our findings, we find that you are not a Convention refugee. I have spoken on behalf of the Panel, but I will ask my colleague Mr. XXXXXXXX if he would like to add anything to the reasons that I have provided for our decision. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, Member I have nothing to add. I concur. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, Presiding Member Thank you, Mr. XXXXXXXX. 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
14 A98-01069 
 Then, again, our determination is that you are not a Convention refugee. You will receive a written copy of this oral decision, which may be edited for grammar, style, presentation in written form, and inclusion, if necessary, of refere nces to jurisprudence, but otherwise would not be in any substantive way different from what you have heard from my mouth this morning. This hearing is concluded. "XXXXXXXXXXXXXX" XXXXXXXXXXXXXX I concur: " G a r y F . M c C a u l e y " G a r y F . M c C a u l e y Dated at Ottawa this 16
th day of November 2000. 
KEYWORDS - REFUGEE DIVISION - CREDIBILITY - MISREPRESENTATION - POLITICAL OPINION - WOMEN REFUGEES – GENDER – PARTI CULAR SOCIAL GROUP – GENDER-RELATED PERSECUTION – DISCRIMINATION - FEMALE - NEGATIVE - DJIBOUTI 
 
2000 CanLII 21315 (CA IRB)
tribunal: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada
